notes.claim: IEC 60229 sets a site test of 4 kV d.c. per millimetre of specified oversheath thickness, at most 10 kV, for 1 minute, between the underlying metallic layers and an outer electrode.
In that standard all metallic layers under the oversheath are connected together, and no breakdown of the oversheath may occur during the test.
The factory routine test in IEC 60229 is stronger: 8 kV d.c. per millimetre for 1 minute, with the underlying metal layer at negative polarity.
Your notes give the same test: screen conductor to earth, 4 kV per mm of sheath thickness up to 10 kV for 1 minute, with conductor, foil and screen connected together.
Your notes say lots of cables have sheath faults, which can cause full cable loss and be very expensive.
IEC 60229 notes that an oversheath can be designed to protect the insulation as well as against corrosion, which is why its integrity matters.

For a sheath that is not semi-conductive, your notes connect negative to the screen conductor and positive to an earth electrode. For a semi-conductive sheath, positive goes through a roll spring to the semi-con layer.
One utility specification calls for a 10 kV d.c. test for 1 minute between sheath and earth where the outer sheath is insulating rather than semi-conducting.
A damaged sheath lets water in. Water that passes through a damaged sheath or joint causes water treeing once the electric field acts on it.

The outer jacket slows the ingress of water and ions from outside. Water trees are tiny branching cavities that grow slowly, over months or years, until the stress at a tip starts an electrical tree and the cable faults. Moisture, a high field, insulation defects and time together promote them.

A utility's guide names failure of the enclosing sheath, and the ingress of water, as a major cause of cable failure, and says actual failure does not come straight after the breach. A commissioning-test review of HV cable says failures are more often due to sheath problems than to the main insulation. That is why a sheath that fails its test matters while the main insulation still passes.

Sheath test levels differ by who sets them: the notes and IEC 60229 give 4 kV per mm up to 10 kV for 1 minute. A distribution network operator uses 10 kV DC for 1 minute on new installation of insulated-sheath cable and 5 kV for 1 minute on 6.6 to 33 kV polymeric cable. A cable maker's guide for medium-voltage cable uses a 1000 V insulation test. Taught as different levels for different cables, with the case using the notes' rule.

The IEC standards for 30 to 500 kV cable (IEC 60840 and IEC 62067) limit their after-installation tests to withstand tests on the main insulation and the sheath. IEC 60840 covers 66 kV cable but leaves submarine cables out of its scope, saying the standard tests may need modifying for them. So the oversheath rule in the notes is the notes' and IEC 60229's, applied to a subsea cable by the course.

The outer face of the sheath needs a conductor for the test voltage to cross the sheath. On land cable a graphite or semi-conducting coating on the sheath gives a continuous potential. A submarine functional specification asks for graphite or an extruded conductive layer on the polyethylene outer sheath to facilitate DC testing of the outer sheath. Voltage goes between the ungrounded screen and the ground, so the screen's earth is taken off for the test.

In a three-core 66 kV array cable each power core has its own polyethylene sheath over its screen. The armour wires and outer polypropylene yarn serving sit outside the three cores. So the sheath test of a three-core cable is made on each core's sheath; no source here describes testing the outer yarn serving, which is open to seawater.

Sheath test sets are made with 10 kV DC outputs of either polarity. The maker's manual says the test object is discharged by the set's discharge device after the test and must be earthed before any contact.

After a sheath test the screens need earthing for time before handling: a cable maker's guide says at least 5 minutes after a sheath insulation test. A case from a 132 kV line is where the screen earths were not put back after the sheath tests and the line ran energised for several days without them.
